executive_summary: The dollar enters September 2026 with the DXY at roughly 99.4-99.5, having failed on 31 August at the 99.75 confluence of the 100-period average and the 38.2% retracement, and with EUR/USD at 1.15902. On DXY weights the basket is down 0.37% over one month and 0.12% over three, but up 0.46% over six and 1.95% over twelve; the Federal Reserve's broad trade-weighted index at 118.7479 fell 1.69% on the month, a wider decline than the G10-only basket, so the dollar has lost more ground against emerging markets than against its peers. The dominant narrative has inverted since the spring: the Federal Reserve is now the only G10 central bank the market expects to RAISE rates. Futures price roughly a 57-66% chance of a 25bp hike on 16 September against a 3.50-3.75% target range, after Chair Warsh used his 28 August Jackson Hole keynote to say that better summer inflation prints do not tell him underlying trends have meaningfully improved, quoting headline PCE at 3.7% and 4.1% annualised over six months, and after a 9-3 July hold in which all three dissenters wanted to hike. Core PCE has been stuck at 3.3% for three months and headline PCE at 3.7%, while the June dot plot already carries a 2026 median of 3.8%. On valuation the dollar is expensive: the BIS real effective rate of 107.84 is the fourth highest in the G10+SGD set and the current account deficit is 2.9% of GDP against a net international investment position of minus $21.27 trillion. The central tension is that the Fed is being pushed to tighten by an inflation problem that is substantially tariff-driven, into a labour market that shed 23,000 payrolls in July with average hourly earnings at a five-year low of 3.2%. We are tactically Bullish the dollar with conviction 3, and strategically Neutral with a bullish tilt at conviction 2 - the September hike is the peak of the story, not the start of it, and the fiscal, external and reserve-share arithmetic reasserts itself beyond it.

valuation.trade_weighted_assessment: The two trade-weighted measures disagree and the disagreement is informative. The G10-only DXY basket is down 0.37% on the month while the Federal Reserve's broad index, which includes emerging markets, is down 1.69% - so the dollar's weakness over August was concentrated against EM rather than against its G10 peers. That is consistent with a market rewarding the US rate advantage inside the G10 while simultaneously reducing structural dollar exposure at the reserve-manager and EM-carry level.
valuation.what_is_priced_in: At a real effective rate of 107.84 the market is pricing a durable US real-yield premium: the 10-year TIPS yield of 2.42% plus a 2.31% breakeven exactly reconciles to the 4.73% nominal, and 2.42% real is a genuinely restrictive level that few peers can match. What is NOT priced is any deterioration in the quality of that premium - the level assumes the US can keep running a 2.9% current account deficit and a deficit above $2 trillion while foreign official holders keep their reserve share near 57%. Valuation is currently a permission slip for tactical dollar strength, not an obstacle to it.
valuation.actionability: This valuation signal is structural, not actionable over two to four weeks: a real effective rate that has moved 0.21 points in a year is not a timing tool. It becomes actionable only in combination with a catalyst that changes the real-yield premium, which is exactly what the 16 September decision and Summary of Economic Projections are.

tactical.analysis: The Federal Reserve is the only central bank in the G10+SGD set that the market expects to raise rates in September, and that single fact dominates this factor. The target range is 3.50-3.75%, a 3.625% midpoint, held on 29 July by a 9-3 vote in which all three dissenters preferred a 25bp increase - the first meeting since September 2016 with three dissents united on direction. Fed funds futures priced roughly 57-66% odds of a hike on 16 September across sources on 31 August, up from 35.4% the day before Chair Warsh's Jackson Hole keynote; prediction markets carry it materially lower at roughly 48-55%, and that venue divergence is itself a tradeable signal. The clean independent confirmation is the 2-year Treasury at 4.34%, which sits 71.5bp above the policy midpoint - a front end that far above the funds rate cannot be reconciled with a hold-then-cut path and embeds both a hike and a higher terminal. On the policy rate the dollar ranks third of ten in the set, behind only Australia at 4.35% and Norway at 4.25%, and it yields more than seven of the ten peers: 137.5bp over the euro and the Canadian dollar, 187.5bp over the Swedish krona, 262.5bp over the yen and 362.5bp over the franc. Sterling is the only peer within 25bp, 12.5bp above, and a September hike flips that differential negative for the first time this cycle. At the long end the picture is less flattering and must be read with care, because every peer 10-year in the cache is a monthly observation dated 2026-06-01 while the US DGS series is current: on a like-for-like June basis the US yields 150bp over Germany, 180bp over Japan, 416bp over Switzerland and 105bp over Canada, but 32.6bp LESS than the UK and 36.1bp less than Australia. The curve is positively sloped with 2s10s at +41bp, 10y3m at +84bp and 2s30s at +88bp, and the 2s10s has flattened 6bp on the month while the 30-year sits at 5.22% - a bear-flattening front end with a term-premium-laden long end, which is precisely what a credible hike into a fiscal problem looks like. Over the next six months the trajectory diverges further: the Fed is the only bank with a hiking bias while the ECB, BoJ, SNB, BoC, RBNZ and Riksbank are all expected to hold and the RBA, Norges Bank and BoE carry easing biases, so the forward carry differential widens rather than narrows.

tactical.what_is_priced: Futures price roughly 57-66% of a September hike and the June dot median of 3.8% implies exactly one. Our view is that the hike happens and that the residual 34-43% not priced is the tradeable gap, because Warsh has staked the Committee's inflation credibility on core PCE and core PCE has not moved for three months. What is NOT priced is the shape after September - the 2027 median of 3.6% implies a cut back, and the market is not distinguishing between a hike that begins a cycle and a hike that ends one.

strategic.analysis: Over one to six months the rate advantage remains real but its rate of change turns against the dollar, which is why confidence falls ten points from the tactical read. The June Summary of Economic Projections carries a 2026 median of 3.8% and a 2027 median of 3.6%: on the Committee's own arithmetic the September hike is the last one, and the following move is a cut. That converts the strategic question from 'does the differential widen' to 'how long does it persist', and the honest answer is that it persists at roughly current levels rather than extending. The 16 September meeting carries a fresh Summary of Economic Projections, so the strategic path will be repriced on the same day the tactical event resolves - an unusually clean information event. Against that, no peer is moving toward the dollar: the ECB has no inflation problem of the US kind and is expected to hold through its 17 December projection round, the SNB is anchored at zero, the BoJ is normalising only gradually with the differential still at 262.5bp, and the Riksbank sits at a 1.75% trough. The two peers that out-yield the dollar are both deteriorating at the margin - Norway's 4.25% is being undermined by Brent falling from $100.31 to $88.24 over the month, and Australia's 4.35% comes with an easing bias building into the 8 December meeting. The structural threat is at the long end rather than the front: the cached Japanese 10-year of 2.67% is a June vintage that materially understates the live level, so the 180bp spread driving USD/JPY at 159.75 is narrower than it appears and narrowing, and that is the single largest carry-unwind risk in the set. Sterling is the specific pair to watch, because a 12.5bp positive differential flipping to 12.5bp negative on 16 September is a rare clean sign change.

carry_analysis.carry_regime: Carry is working, and the regime supports it. Realised volatility is low across the set, the VIX is at 14.43 after falling 6.23 points on the month, investment-grade spreads are at 79bp and high yield at 260bp, and the cross-currency basis is essentially zero - the exact low-volatility, no-funding-stress environment in which carry accrues rather than being wiped out by gap moves. The risk is not that carry stops paying but that it stops mattering: at 5.679% three-month implied volatility, a single 2% gap on a hawkish or dovish FOMC surprise erases more than a year of the 137.5bp EUR/USD carry.
carry_analysis.breakeven_move: Approximately 13 pips over 30 days on EUR/USD. The 137.5bp annual policy differential is worth 159.4 pips a year at a 1.15902 spot, so 13.1 pips over thirty days - spot can rise from 1.15902 to 1.16033 before the carry is erased. The one-month forward outright is 1.16047 with forward points of +14.46, close to but NOT identical with the 13.1-pip policy-differential breakeven: the roughly 1.4-pip gap is the difference between the 137.5bp policy differential and the roughly 150bp the forward actually embeds, which is the policy differential plus the cross-currency basis and the money-market spread. The two are consistent, not equal, and the residual is the basis. The practical consequence is that a long-dollar spot position must clear a hurdle of roughly 1.4-1.5% annualised just to break even against the forward.

tactical.analysis: This factor is genuinely two-sided and the split runs cleanly between prices, which are hawkish, and labour, which is not. On prices the July PCE report published on 26 August was an upside surprise: headline PCE rose 3.7% year on year against a 3.6% forecast and 0.2% on the month against 0.1%, while core PCE - held at 3.3% for a third consecutive month at 0.2% on the month, though it is worth noting that Warsh's Jackson Hole speech cited HEADLINE PCE at 3.7% and its six-month annualised rate of 4.1% as the Fed's preferred measure, not the core series - a framing that is more hawkish than the core number, not less. The quarterly deflators were worse still, with Q2 core PCE prices at 3.6% annualised against a 3.4% forecast and the GDP price index at 6.4% against 6.3%; quarterly-annualised core running above the twelve-month rate is the arithmetic definition of momentum that is not decelerating. CPI tells a softer and genuinely conflicting story - headline 3.4% and core 2.5% in July, both down 0.1 point from June - and the 80bp gap between core PCE at 3.3% and core CPI at 2.5% is an inversion of the usual sign, since core CPI normally runs above core PCE on housing weights. That inversion is the most under-analysed fact in the dossier: it points to tariff pass-through concentrated in the goods and imputed components that PCE weights more heavily, at an average statutory tariff rate of 11.0% as at 24 August 2026, the highest since roughly the early 1940s. Growth is strong on the survey side and weak on the labour side. The August composite PMI printed 56.0 against a 54.0 forecast with services at 56.8 against 53.9, the Philadelphia Fed manufacturing index came in at 47.4 against 24.1, and the Atlanta Fed's GDPNow for the third quarter stands at 4.8% as updated on 1 September, from 4.6% on 26 August after Q2 grew just 1.5% annualised. Against that, July payrolls FELL 23,000 against a consensus of +83,000, government payrolls dropped 53,000, leisure and hospitality shed 40,000, and average hourly earnings slowed to 3.2% year on year, the weakest since May 2021. The unemployment rate fell to 4.1% only because participation fell to 61.4%. Jobless claims at 203,000 and continuing claims at 1,778,000 say this is a low-firing, low-hiring market rather than a recessionary one. For a reaction function anchored on core PCE, the price side dominates over two to four weeks.

tactical.what_is_priced: The market is priced for core PCE to stay near 3.3% and for the Fed to react to it, which is why hike odds sit at 57-66%. What is not priced is the August payroll report on 4 September, forecast at +58,000: a second consecutive negative print would be a far larger shock than an in-line CPI, because it would force the Committee to hike into visible labour-market deterioration two weeks later. We think the price data holds and the labour data is the asymmetric risk, so the tactical skew is dollar-positive but with a fat left tail on 4 September.

strategic.analysis: Over one to six months the balance shifts, which is why the stance moves to Neutral. The inflation that is forcing the Fed's hand is substantially a tariff effect, and a tariff is a level shift in prices rather than a persistent inflation process: an average statutory rate of 11.0% raises the price index once and then drops out of the year-on-year comparison. The Supreme Court struck down the IEEPA tariffs on 20 February 2026 and the successor 10% global tariff was imposed under Section 122 of the Trade Act for a 150-day period from 24 February, expiring on 24 July; Section 301 duties of 10-12.5% on roughly 80 trading partners took effect that same day, so the structure transitioned rather than lapsed - but it did so onto an authority that is narrower, country-specific and more exposed to challenge. If that structure is unwound or refunded, the goods component of core PCE deflates mechanically. Meanwhile the labour market deterioration compounds rather than reverses on a six-month view: payrolls at -23,000, wage growth at a five-year low of 3.2%, participation falling to 61.4% and ISM non-manufacturing employment at 47.4 are not a one-month artefact. The consumer is visibly slowing, with Conference Board confidence at 89.4 against 90.3 expected, Michigan sentiment down to 51.7 from 55.2, new home sales down 10.5% on the month and retail sales at -0.6%. The offsetting bull case is real: GDPNow at 4.8%, composite PMI at 56.0 and corporate profits up 8.2% on the quarter describe an economy with genuine nominal momentum. But growth of that quality alongside decelerating wages and falling participation is a productivity story, not a demand story, and productivity-led growth is disinflationary. Michigan one-year inflation expectations already fell to 4.0% from 4.2%, and five-to-ten-year expectations are stable at 3.3% with market breakevens anchored at 2.31%. On a six-month view the forces genuinely offset.

factors.horizon_split_explanation: The stance changes from Bullish to Neutral because the two sides of this factor operate on different clocks. Tactically the Fed reacts to the last core PCE print, which was 3.3% and unmoved, and that is what determines the 16 September outcome. Strategically the tariff component that is doing most of the work in core PCE is a level effect with a defined and legally uncertain life, while the labour deterioration is a trend - so the same data set that is hawkish over four weeks is ambiguous over six months.

tactical.analysis: For the dollar this factor's sign convention inverts relative to every other currency in the set, and stating that explicitly matters more than the reading itself. The dollar is the risk-off beneficiary: a VIX spike is dollar-POSITIVE, and a benign risk environment is dollar-negative through the carry-outflow channel. The current environment is emphatically benign. The VIX closed at 14.43 on 28 August, down 6.23 points from 20.66 a month earlier - a collapse, not a drift. Investment-grade option-adjusted spreads are at 79bp and high yield at 260bp, the latter having tightened 27bp on the month; both are close to post-crisis tights and neither leaves any cushion. On the dollar smile framework the currency is not on the left-hand, funding-stress side - the cross-currency basis proves that, sitting essentially at zero - but it is also not at the bottom, because US exceptionalism is live: GDPNow at 4.8%, composite PMI at 56.0 and the only G10 central bank expected to tighten all place the dollar on the right-hand slope. Those two forces genuinely offset, which is what makes Neutral the honest stance rather than a hedge. The correlation structure is behaving oddly and deserves attention: gold speculative net length rose to 243.3k contracts from 222.2k while the dollar firmed, and the two do not normally rally together. Gold bid alongside a firm dollar is a debasement hedge rather than a dollar-alternative trade, which is consistent with the fiscal and reserve-share themes in Factors 5 and 8. Equity positioning has flipped hard in the other direction: S&P 500 speculative net positions swung to -68.0k on 28 August from -10.6k a week earlier and +11.3k two weeks before that. The 1 September session is the first evidence of transmission, with a global bond rout lifting yields, gold to a ten-day low and equities lower while crude rebounded on Middle East risk. Tail scenarios that would flip this factor hard dollar-positive are a credit repricing from 79bp investment grade, an Asian long-end disorder episode, and a Middle East escalation that closes shipping.

tactical.what_is_priced: The market is priced for calm: a 14.43 VIX, 79bp investment-grade spreads and 5.679% three-month FX implied volatility all say the same thing. For the dollar that calm is a mild negative through the carry-outflow channel, and it is priced. What is not priced is the asymmetry - from these levels the distribution of VIX outcomes is overwhelmingly skewed higher, and every point of that skew is dollar-positive, so this factor is a cheap embedded call option on the long-dollar view rather than a drag.

strategic.analysis: Over one to six months the same offsetting structure holds but with lower confidence, because the identity of the marginal risk driver becomes less predictable. The strategic case for a dollar-positive risk regime rests on the observation that credit and equity volatility cannot get much cheaper: at 79bp investment grade and 260bp high yield, the compensation for credit risk is close to its floor, and the mean-reverting path from there is wider spreads, which is dollar-positive. The strategic case against is that a synchronised global expansion - which composite PMIs at 56 in the US, Swedish growth at 3.3% year on year and Singaporean growth at 5.9% all point toward - is the classic bottom-of-the-smile configuration in which capital leaves the dollar for higher-beta destinations, and that is exactly what the broad trade-weighted index falling 1.69% on the month while the G10 basket fell only 0.37% is describing. The dollar lost ground to emerging markets, not to its peers. Correlation structure is the thing to monitor: the historical dollar-versus-S&P relationship of -0.2 to -0.4 in goldilocks and +0.2 to +0.4 in crisis is the tell for which side of the smile is active, and gold rallying with the dollar suggests the standard structure is already partially broken. Over six months there are three identifiable regime-shift candidates - a US labour recession confirmed by two more negative payroll prints, a Middle East escalation that reprices energy, and a long-end disorder episode with the 30-year already at 5.22%. The first is dollar-negative and the second and third are dollar-positive, which is why the honest strategic stance is Neutral rather than a directional bet on any one of them.

factors.horizon_split_explanation: Both horizons are Neutral because the risk-off benefit to the dollar and the carry-outflow cost of calm genuinely offset, but confidence falls from 55 to 52 because the strategic identity of the marginal risk driver is less determinable. Mechanically the tactical read is anchored on observable current levels - a 14.43 VIX and 79bp spreads - while the strategic read depends on which of three unrelated regime-shift candidates arrives first, and two of them point one way and one the other.

tactical.analysis: The positioning read is that the dollar is net long but the length has been coming off for a month, and critically it came off BEFORE the catalyst rather than after it. CFTC non-commercial net length in the US Dollar Index contract peaked at 22,499 contracts on 4 August 2026, described in the weekly summaries as around a three-and-a-half-year high, and has declined for four consecutive weeks: 21,409 on 11 August, 19,079 on 18 August and 18,682 on 25 August, a cumulative reduction of 3,817 contracts or roughly 17% of the peak. Warsh spoke on 28 August, after the last of those tranches, so the market entered the most hawkish central-bank communication of the year with a lighter book than it carried at the start of the month. That is close to the opposite of the crowded-long-into-a-catalyst configuration that usually makes positioning dangerous, and it is why the stance is Neutral rather than Bearish despite an elevated absolute level. A significant methodological caveat applies: the pipeline's cached Commitments of Traders file contains no Dollar Index contract at all, so every figure here is web-sourced rather than cache-sourced, and the DXY contract is reported as non-commercial versus commercial rather than with the leveraged-fund and asset-manager split available for the major bilateral contracts - the same non-commercial net figure therefore appears in both fields and that is a reporting limitation rather than two independent observations. The percentile of roughly 80 is an internal estimate anchored on the reported three-and-a-half-year-high reference point and is not a published statistic. Open interest in the DXY contract is small relative to EUR, JPY and GBP futures, which matters for a practical reason: any unwind would be transmitted through the bilateral pairs rather than through the index. Adjacent CFTC series show a genuine risk-reduction impulse in the same week, with S&P 500 net positions at -68.0k from -10.6k. UUP and UDN exchange-traded fund flows were not obtainable from any free source and are recorded as a gap; 25-delta risk reversals are likewise unavailable, so the options-hedging channel is uninformed rather than neutral.

tactical.what_is_priced: Positioning is priced as mildly long and getting less so, which is what the four-week decline shows. Our read is that the market has under-appreciated the timing: because the length came off before Jackson Hole rather than after it, the post-Warsh repricing was absorbed by a lighter book and the squeeze risk into 16 September is lower than the absolute net long number implies. The corollary is that there is room to add, which is a mild tactical positive rather than the contrarian negative that an 80th-percentile reading would normally signal.

strategic.analysis: Over one to six months positioning turns from a neutral to a negative for the dollar, because the relevant flow question stops being weekly speculative futures and becomes the structural allocation decision of reserve managers and long-term asset allocators. On that measure the direction is unambiguous and one-way: the dollar's share of allocated global foreign exchange reserves stood at 57.13% in the first quarter of 2026, having RISEN from 56.42% in the fourth quarter of 2025 - the quarter that was itself the first sub-57% reading since 1995 - against a 2001 peak near 72%. The important nuance, and the reason confidence is low, is twofold: the latest quarter actually went the OTHER way, with the share rising 0.71 percentage points, and the IMF has attributed the majority of past declines to valuation artefacts rather than active selling - in the second quarter of 2025 the IMF attributed 92% of the fall to exchange-rate effects rather than to central banks changing their portfolios, and that figure is five quarters old. So de-dollarisation is real but slow, and it is a drag rather than a driver. The starting point matters too: entering the strategic window from a three-and-a-half-year high in speculative length means the medium-term distribution of positioning change is skewed toward reduction rather than accumulation, since there is far more room to sell than to buy. The broad trade-weighted index falling 1.69% on the month while the G10-only basket fell 0.37% is the flow signature of exactly this - structural dollar exposure being reduced at the EM and reserve-manager level while tactical G10 carry positions are maintained. Working against the bearish read is the mechanical demand created by a widening current account deficit that must be financed and by the dollar's roughly 40-50% share of global trade invoicing, which generates structural demand independent of any allocation decision, plus the Treasury International Capital release on 16 September showing net long-term transactions of $172.7bn previously. On balance the structural flow direction is negative, but at low conviction.

factors.horizon_split_explanation: The stance moves from Neutral to Bearish because the two horizons measure different flows. Tactically the relevant flow is four weeks of speculative futures reduction into a catalyst, which is benign. Strategically the relevant flow is reserve-manager allocation and the starting level of speculative length, both of which point one way - down - and the mechanism is that a three-and-a-half-year-high starting point plus a structurally eroding reserve share leaves far more room for positions to be reduced than added.
factors.contrarian_analysis_tactical: Positioning is elevated in absolute terms at roughly the 80th percentile but is NOT stretched in the way that matters, because the length has been falling for four consecutive weeks and all of that reduction happened before the 28 August catalyst. The unwind trigger is narrow and specific: a hold on 16 September, against 57-66% odds of a hike, would strand an 18,682-contract net long in a market that repriced from 35.4% to 60.4% in four sessions. The squeeze would be violent but short - the DXY contract's small open interest means it would be transmitted through EUR/USD and USD/JPY, and we would expect a 1.5-2.5% dollar decline within a week, taking EUR/USD toward the 1.17275-1.17759 supply zone. The other side of the trade is being taken by prediction-market participants, who price the hike at roughly 48-55% against futures at 57-66%, and by anyone who believes the July payroll print of -23,000 makes tightening politically and analytically indefensible; that is a coherent position, not a lazy one, and it is why the tactical stance is Neutral rather than Bullish.
factors.contrarian_analysis_strategic: Over one to six months the contrarian question inverts: the crowd is not long the dollar, it is short it. The published sell-side consensus points to a DXY in the mid-90s by end-2026 from roughly 99.4, with MUFG expecting a further 5% decline in a note dated 19 December 2025 that is already directionally falsified, and aggregator-reported forecasts placing Morgan Stanley's 94 at mid-2026 with a 99 year-end recovery and Natixis near 98 - and the stated driver in those write-ups is 'an expected sequence of Fed rate cuts in 2026', a premise the June dot plot, the 9-3 July vote and a 4.34% 2-year have already falsified. The contrarian strategic trade is therefore to be less bearish the dollar than the HEADLINE consensus, not more - though on inspection the consensus is less bearish than it is reported to be, since Morgan Stanley's year-end 99 is essentially spot and only MUFG's genuinely bearish call is first-party sourced, and that one is eight months old. What would trigger the consensus unwind is a September hike followed by a hawkish Summary of Economic Projections, which would force forecast revisions through October. Against that, the structural flow case is genuinely one-way: a reserve share still roughly 15 percentage points below its 2001 peak, a three-and-a-half-year-high starting position and a deficit above $2 trillion all argue that any dollar rally is a selling opportunity for real money, which is precisely why our strategic stance on this factor is Bearish even though we think the consensus level is wrong.

tactical.analysis: At a 0.06 tactical weight this factor is a background reading, and over two to four weeks the external accounts do not move spot - which is the honest reason for a Neutral stance rather than an attempt to read direction into slow data. The current account deficit widened by $5.8bn or 2.6% to $226.8bn in the first quarter of 2026, taking it to 2.9% of GDP from 2.8% in the fourth quarter, and the cached OECD point-in-time vintage corroborates at -2.85%. The composition is what changed: the widening reflected the primary income balance flipping from surplus to deficit, partly offset by a smaller goods deficit - and the primary income balance turning negative is genuinely notable, because the 'exorbitant privilege' of earning more on foreign assets than is paid on foreign liabilities is the mechanism that has made a minus $21.27 trillion net international investment position sustainable. The tactical datapoint that actually matters is the advance goods trade balance published on 27 August at minus $118.8bn against a minus $100.8bn forecast and a minus $101.4bn prior - an $18bn single-month deterioration and a large miss, with the full trade balance due on 3 September forecast at minus $86.4bn against minus $73.3bn. On commodities the dollar's exposure is mild and mixed. The US is now a net energy exporter, so Brent falling from $100.31 to $88.24 and WTI to $83.90 over the month is a modest terms-of-trade negative, though it is a substantial positive for the inflation path and therefore cuts against the hike. Henry Hub at $2.70 is unremarkable. Crude was rebounding on 1 September on Middle East risk. Trade policy is where the real action is: the average statutory tariff rate is 11.0% as at 24 August 2026, the highest since roughly the early 1940s, having come down from 16% before the Supreme Court struck down the IEEPA tariffs and the structure transitioned onto Section 301 authority on 24 July. Over four weeks none of this moves the dollar; over six months all of it does.

tactical.what_is_priced: Nothing in the external accounts is priced over a four-week horizon, and correctly so - a quarterly current account release does not move a currency in September. strategic.analysis: At a 0.16 strategic weight this is the second most important factor on the one-to-six-month horizon and it is unambiguously negative for the dollar. The arithmetic is straightforward and it compounds: a current account deficit of 2.9% of GDP that is widening, a net international investment position of minus $21.27 trillion, a goods trade balance that deteriorated $18bn in a single month, and a reserve share of 57.13% that, while it ROSE in the latest quarter from 56.42%, sits far below the 2001 peak near 72%. The composition change is the part that deserves emphasis. The primary income balance flipping from surplus to deficit in the first quarter attacks the specific mechanism - higher returns on US foreign assets than foreign investors earn on US assets - that has allowed a deeply negative net investment position to coexist with a stable currency for two decades. If that flips durably, the deficit stops being self-financing on favourable terms. Trade policy is the second strategic negative and it is genuinely unresolved. The Supreme Court held on 20 February 2026 by 6-3 in Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump that the International Emergency Economic Powers Act does not authorise the President to impose tariffs, striking down the reciprocal and trafficking tariffs. The administration responded within hours with a 10% global tariff under Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974, effective 24 February for 150 days - a window that on its face closed around 24 July - and launched Section 301 investigations as the successor authority. Those succeeded cleanly rather than leaving a vacuum: following the USTR determination of 2 June 2026, Section 301 duties of 10-12.5% on roughly 80 trading partners took effect on 24 July 2026, the same day the Section 122 authority lapsed, with Section 232 actions running in parallel. Importers who paid IEEPA tariffs may be entitled to refunds whose mechanics remain unannounced. An average statutory tariff rate of 11.0% is simultaneously an inflation impulse, a fiscal revenue stream of uncertain durability, a contingent refund liability and a legal question, and the resolution of that question over the next six months is a genuine dollar risk in both directions. On the offsetting side, the dollar's roughly 40-50% share of global trade invoicing generates structural demand regardless of the trade balance, and the reserve-share decline is mostly valuation rather than active selling.

tactical.analysis: The Federal Reserve's communication over the past ten weeks has been consistently and increasingly hawkish, and the market has been repricing toward it rather than away from it. The June Summary of Economic Projections raised the 2026 median federal funds rate to 3.8% from 3.4% in March - a median that already implies one hike from the current 3.625% midpoint - while lifting the 2026 median headline PCE projection to 3.6% from 2.7% and core PCE to 3.3% from 2.7%. Nine participants backed continued hikes in 2026. The July meeting then delivered a 9-3 hold in which all three dissenters explicitly preferred a 25bp increase, the first three-dissent meeting with a unified direction since September 2016; a vote of that shape is a stronger guidance signal than any statement language, because it reveals how close the Committee is to moving. Chair Warsh then used the 28 August Jackson Hole keynote to close the gap, giving a more hawkish reading of inflation than he had after the July meeting, recommitting to the 2% PCE objective as the 'firm, fixed target', citing the twelve-month change in the HEADLINE PCE price index at 3.7% and its six-month change at 4.1% as the Fed's preferred measure of inflation, and stating that while the summer's inflation readings were better than expected they do not tell him that underlying trends have meaningfully improved. The speech must be read precisely, and reading it precisely cuts both ways: it explicitly disclaims forward guidance, never names September or a direction, describes the labour market as consistent with full employment, and does not use the word tariff once - so it is a commitment to a reaction function rather than a pre-announcement. Markets moved immediately, with FedWatch hike odds going from 35.4% to roughly 57.5% on the day and 60.4% by 31 August. The guidance-versus-pricing gap is therefore small but pointed in one direction: the Committee's own median implies a hike with certainty while the market prices 57-66%, so the market is BELOW the dots rather than above them - the unusual configuration in which the central bank is more hawkish than the curve. The credibility question here is inverted from the normal one. The risk is not that markets doubt Warsh's hawkishness but that they doubt his independence, and the analyst commentary after Jackson Hole framed the speech as putting the Fed at odds with the Treasury. The 16 September decision resolves that in one direction or the other, with fresh projections attached.

strategic.analysis: Over one to six months the guidance story remains net positive for the dollar but the confidence falls eleven points, because the strategic risk in Federal Reserve communication right now is institutional rather than analytical. The mechanical case is unchanged: the June dot plot's 2026 median of 3.8% is above market pricing, the 16 September meeting carries a fresh Summary of Economic Projections that will reset the strategic path, and the Committee has demonstrated with a 9-3 vote that its internal distribution has a hawkish tail. The Fed has also moved from calendar-based to meeting-by-meeting data dependence, which raises event-by-event volatility and means each of the 16 September, 28 October and 9 December decisions is a genuine repricing opportunity rather than a formality. The strategic complication is the political overlay, and it cuts in an unusual direction. Trump has publicly said interest rates are 'too high' and the US 'should be paying much less', but has notably exempted Warsh - whom he nominated - from the criticism he directs at other Fed officials, saying Warsh is doing a 'great job' and will 'do what he has to do'. Analysts have framed the Jackson Hole speech as putting the Fed 'at odds' with the Treasury and have argued explicitly that hiking would DEMONSTRATE independence, since credibility depends on the ability to raise rates over a president's objections. That is a reflexive and self-reinforcing argument: a central bank under political pressure to cut has an institutional incentive to tighten when inflation justifies it, and we do not believe the market has priced that reflexivity. The offsetting strategic risk is real - if the market ever concludes that the reaction function is politically rather than analytically determined, the dollar loses the credibility premium that S&P explicitly cited when affirming the AA+ rating on 26 June. That is a low-probability, high-severity scenario and it is the reason confidence is 55 rather than 65.

tactical.analysis: Over two to four weeks the event calendar is unusually dense and its balance tilts dollar-positive, which is what makes a Bullish stance appropriate at a modest 0.05 weight. The dominant event is the 16 September FOMC decision with a Summary of Economic Projections attached - a genuine binary carrying 57-66% odds of a hike in futures against roughly 48-55% in prediction markets, with a dot plot released simultaneously that resets the whole forward path. Before it, the 4 September August payroll report (consensus +58,000 after -23,000) and the 11 September CPI release are both first-order, and after it the Bank of England on 17 September and the Bank of Japan on 18 September resolve within two days, so the entire G10 policy complex reprices inside a 72-hour window. For the dollar, escalation is a positive on both channels simultaneously: safe-haven demand and, as a net energy exporter, a terms-of-trade gain. The tariff situation is a live legal event rather than a settled policy, since the Section 122 authority underpinning the 10% global tariff expired on 24 July and was replaced the same day by Section 301 duties of 10-12.5%, whose durability and scope are still being litigated and negotiated. An OPEC meeting on 6 September sits directly in the window. Tail scenarios that would move the dollar more than 2% are a Middle East escalation closing shipping, a hold-plus-dovish-dots surprise on 16 September, and a long-end disorder episode from a 5.22% 30-year.

strategic.analysis: Over one to six months the event balance becomes genuinely two-sided, which is why the stance is Neutral. The dominant scheduled event in the strategic window is the US midterm congressional elections on 3 November 2026, and their FX implication is ambiguous in a way that resists a directional stance: a result that constrains fiscal expansion would be dollar-positive through the deficit channel and dollar-negative through the growth channel, while a result that enables it would be the reverse, and the second-order question of how either outcome affects political pressure on the Federal Reserve is unknowable in advance. The tariff question resolves inside this window rather than the tactical one. With Section 122 authority lapsed on 24 July 2026 and Section 301 duties of 10-12.5% having taken effect the same day, the six-month path runs through either the consolidation of that Section 301 architecture - inflationary, hawkish, dollar-positive in the short run and negative for the trade balance thereafter - or an unwind with refunds, which would be disinflationary, remove the case for further tightening, and create a contingent fiscal liability of uncertain size. Both are plausible and they point opposite ways. Geopolitically the Middle East remains the live theatre and the dollar benefits from escalation on both the haven and the energy-export channels, but the base case over six months is de-escalation rather than escalation, and the mean-reversion of Brent from a $105.32 July peak through $100.31 to $88.24 is consistent with that. The US-China relationship, Taiwan and the sanctions architecture are all slow-burning and none has a dated catalyst inside the window. On balance, one large ambiguous scheduled event, one large unresolved legal question that cuts both ways, and a geopolitical backdrop whose base case is quiet - that is the definition of Neutral rather than a hedge.

tactical.analysis: The US fiscal position is deteriorating on every measure that matters, but over two to four weeks it is not currently transmitting to the dollar in the direction the arithmetic implies - which is why the stance is Bearish at the lowest confidence in the dossier. The numbers first: the Treasury has confirmed $1.8 trillion of borrowing over the first ten months of fiscal 2026, the Congressional Budget Office projects $1.9 trillion for the full year, and Treasury run-rate figures suggest the outturn exceeds $2 trillion. Debt held by the public is 101% of GDP in 2026 and projected to reach 120% by 2036, above the post-war record of 106%, with gross debt approaching $40 trillion. Interest costs are the sharpest datapoint, and they are a PROJECTION rather than an outturn because fiscal 2026 does not close until 30 September: the Congressional Budget Office projects $1,039 billion for the year, which would exceed the post-war high of 3.2% of GDP set in 1991, and $2.1 trillion by 2036. The bond market is charging for it at the long end. The 30-year is at 5.22% with 2s30s at +88bp, the 20-year auction on 19 August stopped at 5.204% against 5.163% previously, the 30-year TIPS auction cleared at 2.973% against 2.473% - a 50bp jump - and the 7-year at 4.512% against 4.473%. The August quarterly refunding raised $28.7bn of new cash from a $125 billion package. Yet the tactical transmission is the opposite of the intuitive one: on 1 September a global bond rout pushed yields up, gold to a ten-day low and equities lower, and the dollar was firm. That is yields driving the currency, not fiscal panic driving it - and it means that in the current regime a widening deficit expressed through higher long yields is dollar-supportive rather than dollar-destructive. Ratings are stable and provide no near-term catalyst: Moody's Aa1 since the May 2025 downgrade, S&P AA+ affirmed with a stable outlook on 26 June 2026, Fitch AA+ stable. No rating-agency page was directly fetchable, so those outlooks are best available and flagged.

strategic.analysis: Over one to six months the fiscal position becomes a materially larger drag and confidence rises fourteen points, because the mechanism that currently neutralises it - higher yields attracting capital - is the same mechanism that eventually breaks it. Projected interest costs of $1,039 billion in fiscal 2026, which would exceed the post-war high of 3.2% of GDP, are a record in prospect rather than in fact - the fiscal year closes on 30 September - and they compound: every quarter of low-coupon debt rolling into a 4.5-5.2% curve raises the run-rate mechanically, independent of any policy decision. If the Federal Reserve hikes on 16 September, the front end of that rollover repricing gets worse, which is the specific and under-appreciated interaction between Factor 1 and this one - the policy tightening that supports the dollar tactically raises the fiscal burden that undermines it strategically. Bond supply is the transmission channel to watch. With a deficit above $2 trillion, an August refunding raising $28.7bn of new cash from a $125 billion package, and the overnight reverse repo facility drained to $702 million, heavy bill issuance now hits bank reserves directly rather than being absorbed by money market funds parked at the Fed. Auction reception is already deteriorating at the long end. The rating backdrop is stable, which is a genuine offset - S&P's 26 June affirmation at AA+ explicitly cited 'credible, effective monetary policy execution' and fiscal deficits that are high but not rising - and a September hike would reinforce exactly the credibility S&P priced. The deeper strategic point is the interaction with Factor 5: a deficit above $2 trillion and record interest costs are financeable so long as foreign official holders keep absorbing the paper, and their reserve share touched a three-decade low of 56.42% in 2025-Q4 before rebounding to 57.13%. Neither fact alone moves the dollar; together they are the twin-deficit configuration in which fiscal gravity actually applies.

tactical.analysis: For a dollar dossier this factor is domestic and first-order rather than an external spillover channel, and it must be analysed from the supply side: how is the Federal Reserve affecting global dollar availability? The headline answer over two to four weeks is that dollars are freely available and there is no funding premium anywhere, which is a mild dollar negative - and that is why the stance is Neutral rather than Bullish, despite an asymmetric setup underneath. The definitive evidence is the cross-currency basis. CME's three-month cross-currency basis index for EUR/USD closed at minus 0.81 basis points on 28 August, having ranged between roughly minus 0.81 and plus 0.71 over the month. That is essentially zero. Stressed periods run minus 40 to minus 80 basis points, so the market is not paying anything at all to obtain dollars - which places the dollar unambiguously on the right-hand, US-exceptionalism side of the smile rather than the left-hand, funding-stress side. SOFR is reported near 3.65%, consistent with a 3.50-3.75% target range with no dislocation, and there is no reported swap-line usage. The New York Fed's SOFR landing page is JavaScript-rendered and returned no values to this run, so the specific level is best available and flagged; the daily series is machine-readable on FRED. Quantitative tightening is over: the FOMC announced the cessation of runoff on 29 October 2025 and balance-sheet runoff actually ended on 1 December 2025, after which the New York Desk guided to roughly $40 billion of Treasury bill purchases over the first month with the pace likely maintained toward mid-April - guidance rather than a committed programme, and the pace was subsequently reduced. Only about half of the pandemic balance sheet expansion was ever reversed. The asymmetry sits beneath all of this. The overnight reverse repo facility is drained to $702 million on a Wednesday basis, from a $2.55 trillion peak in December 2022, so the shock absorber that offset three years of tightening is gone, and September quarter-end falls inside the tactical window.

tactical.what_is_priced: The market prices dollar funding as abundant and it is right - a basis of minus 0.81 basis points is as close to a statement of no stress as the instrument can make. What is not priced is the fragility of that condition: reserves at $2,916 billion with no reverse repo buffer left and heavy bill supply from a deficit above $2 trillion is precisely the configuration that produced the widest SOFR-IORB spreads since 2020 last December. We hold Neutral because there is no stress today, but the distribution around quarter-end is skewed dollar-positive.

strategic.analysis: Over one to six months the same setup becomes directional and the stance turns Bullish, because the strategic window contains the specific seasonal and supply conditions under which reserve scarcity actually bites. The mechanism is well documented by the immediately preceding cycle: in the fourth quarter of 2025 SOFR-to-interest-on-reserve-balances spreads reached their widest since 2020, reserve balances fell to levels policymakers judged barely sufficient, and standing repo usage print $25.95 billion on 29 December and spike to a record $74.6 billion on 31 December 2025, before collapsing to zero in early January once year-end passed. Every one of the preconditions for a repeat is in place and several are worse. Reserves are drifting down again at $2,916 billion toward the roughly $3 trillion threshold. The reverse repo facility, which absorbed the drain for three years, is empty at about $1 billion. Bill supply from a deficit above $2 trillion now hits bank reserves directly rather than being intermediated by money funds parked at the Fed. And if the Committee hikes on 16 September, the whole complex reprices upward at the same time. The countervailing force is institutional and it is a genuine one: the New York Fed rebranded the facility as 'standing repo operations' on 10 December 2025 specifically to reduce stigma and drive usage, and eliminated the aggregate limit in favour of full allotment subject to a $40 billion per-proposition cap. That is a permanent backstop upgrade which caps the tail of any squeeze - it makes a funding crisis less likely without making funding pressure less likely. So the strategic call is for a repeat of periodic year-end funding tightness rather than for a dislocation, and tighter dollar funding pushes the currency toward the left-hand side of the smile, which is dollar-positive. Confidence is 55 rather than higher precisely because the backstop works.

The reinforcing chain is clean: Factor 6 at +0.0434 adds the guidance leg, because the June dot plot's 2026 median of 3.8% implies a hike outright while futures price only 57-66%, so the central bank is currently more hawkish than the curve - the reverse of the usual configuration and the single clearest mispricing we can identify. Factor 7 at +0.0260 adds the event leg, and Factor 9 at +0.0270 adds a structural tilt with spot sitting exactly on the 1.15904 zone boundary. The conflicts are real and they are what caps conviction at 3 rather than 4. Factor 8 is negative because the fiscal arithmetic is deteriorating, though it is currently transmitting backwards - the 1 September bond rout lifted yields and the dollar together. Factor 3, Factor 4, Factor 5 and Factor 10 are all Neutral, and Factor 10 in particular is a suppressed dollar positive: a cross-currency basis of minus 0.81 basis points says there is no funding premium at all, which is mildly dollar-negative today even though reserves at $2,916 billion with a reverse repo facility drained to $702 million make the distribution around quarter-end dollar-favourable. The edge is not the direction, which is widely understood; it is the magnitude and the expression. Futures price a hike at 57-66% while the Committee's own median implies it outright, and the volatility term structure is in contango at 5.357/5.679/5.834 fifteen days before an FOMC meeting with a Summary of Economic Projections attached - a market that feared this event would show near-dated backwardation. The path of least resistance is therefore a grind lower in EUR/USD through the 1.15125-1.15904 demand zone toward 1.1450-1.1480, with the DXY reclaiming the 100 handle it lost on 30 July. The catalysts are dated and dense: August payrolls on 4 September with a +58,000 consensus after a -23,000 print, CPI on 11 September, the decision and dot plot on 16 September, then the Bank of England on 17 September and the Bank of Japan on 18 September within 72 hours. The view is highly actionable but the vehicle matters more than usual: a long-dollar spot position must clear roughly 1.4-1.5% annualised just to break even against the forward, whereas the same view bought through options costs a 0.72-point volatility premium once. That asymmetry, not the directional call, is where the money is.

The second leg is a renewed dollar bid from late November into year-end, driven not by rates but by funding - reserves drifting toward $3 trillion with no reverse repo buffer left and heavy bill supply reproduce the December 2025 configuration, and that episode moved the dollar without moving the policy rate. Between and beneath both legs runs a persistent structural sell from reserve managers and the mechanical 1.4% annualised forward give-back, which is why the window ends roughly where the forwards already put it. The shape is a broad U or a double top rather than a trend, volatility should rise from a 5.834% six-month implied that prices no event premium at all, and the level to watch on the downside is 1.16339, the 200-day, above which the tangled moving-average configuration flips against the dollar.

risk_reward.base_case_payoff: -60 pips on EUR/USD, roughly -0.5% on the primary pair, taking spot from 1.15902 to 1.1650 - essentially the outcome the forward curve already prices
risk_reward.downside_case_loss: -450 pips, roughly -3.9%, taking spot from 1.15902 to 1.2050
risk_reward.risk_reward_ratio: 0.76:1 measured on upside against downside (+340 pips against -450 pips); the base case itself is a small negative, so there is no favourable ratio to quote on it
risk_reward.asymmetry_assessment: The strategic distribution is skewed AGAINST the dollar: the downside case loses 450 pips while the upside case gains 340, and the base case is itself a mild loss that simply matches the forward. Probability-weighted expectancy is roughly -58 pips. This is precisely why the strategic stance is Neutral at conviction 2 rather than a diluted version of the tactical Bullish - the arithmetic does not support carrying a long-dollar position through the whole window, and an investor should treat the tactical view as a trade with an expiry rather than as the start of a strategic position.

consensus_divergence.consensus_view: The published sell-side consensus is bearish the dollar and points to a DXY in the mid-90s by the end of 2026, from roughly 99.4-99.5 now, with a forecast range of approximately 92 to 100 for the second half of the year. MUFG, in a note dated 19 December 2025 and therefore well outside this dossier's 60-day strategic freshness window, expected a further 5.0% decline on a DXY basis and EUR/USD at 1.2400 by end-2026; the DXY has in fact risen roughly 1.5% from its 97.96 close for 2025, so that call is already directionally falsified; aggregator-reported forecasts place Morgan Stanley's trough near 94 at MID-2026 with a recovery to 99 by year-end - essentially spot, and the mid-year trough did not in fact occur - and Natixis at 98 by end-2026. Critically, the stated driver in these write-ups is 'an expected sequence of Fed rate cuts in 2026'.
consensus_divergence.our_view: We are tactically Bullish the dollar with conviction 3 and strategically Neutral with a bullish tilt at conviction 2, expecting EUR/USD near 1.1465 in one month and near 1.1650 in six. Our divergence from consensus is largest over the next four weeks and narrows substantially thereafter, which is itself the point: we do not think the consensus level is wrong so much as its stated premise is obsolete.
consensus_divergence.divergence_magnitude: Roughly 4-5 DXY points against the mid-90s headline characterisation on the tactical horizon, though materially less against Morgan Stanley's actual year-end 99 - consensus points toward the mid-90s while we expect the 100 handle to be reclaimed in September - narrowing to approximately 1-2 points over six months as our strategic Neutral converges toward the consensus direction if not its magnitude.
consensus_divergence.why_we_differ: The divergence is about a premise, not a forecast. The consensus write-ups we can source explicitly attribute dollar weakness to expected Fed rate cuts in 2026, and that premise has been falsified four separate ways: the June dot plot raised the 2026 median to 3.8% from 3.4%, the July meeting produced a 9-3 hold in which all three dissenters wanted to HIKE, Chair Warsh used Jackson Hole on 28 August to say underlying inflation trends have not meaningfully improved and to quote headline PCE at 3.7% with a 4.1% six-month annualised rate, and the 2-year Treasury at 4.34% sits 71.5bp above the policy midpoint. A forecast anchored to a rate path the market has already abandoned is not a view we need to argue against on its merits. The market underweights three things specifically: the reflexive dynamic by which political pressure to cut makes a hike MORE likely because the institutional cost of appearing to yield exceeds the economic cost of 25bp; the inverted core CPI to core PCE wedge, where core PCE at 3.3% sits 80bp ABOVE core CPI at 2.5% and it is core PCE the Fed targets; and the fact that reserve balances at $2,916 billion with a reverse repo facility drained to $702 million reproduce the December 2025 funding configuration. We should also state the honest caveat: only the MUFG figure has a first-party source, and the Morgan Stanley and Natixis numbers are aggregator-reported, so the consensus we are diverging from is itself imperfectly observed.
consensus_divergence.payoff_if_right: A tactical dollar rally of 1.1-2.1% on EUR/USD into and through 16 September, with the largest single-day payoff on the statement and dot plot. Expressed through one-month options at a 5.357% implied volatility that carries only a 0.72-point premium over realised, the payoff is materially larger per unit of risk than the spot move suggests, because the market is not charging for the event.
consensus_divergence.risk_if_wrong: If consensus is right and the Fed holds on 16 September, the 18,682-contract net long is stranded into a market that repriced from 35.4% to 60.4% in four sessions, and EUR/USD squeezes 140 pips or more to the 1.17275-1.17759 supply zone within a week. The strategic risk is worse and different: if the hike is delivered but proves a policy mistake into a labour market already shedding payrolls, the dollar gets the tactical rally and then gives back 450 pips as the Fed reverses.

cleanest_bullish_expression.rationale: USD/CAD offers the best combination of carry, volatility and structure for a long-dollar view. It pays 137.5bp of policy carry on the lowest realised volatility in the G10 at 4.07%, a carry-to-volatility ratio of 0.338 that is bettered only by CHF and JPY, both of which carry far more spot risk. Spot at 1.38554 sits almost exactly on the 200-day average of 1.38386, so the entry is at fair value rather than extended, the 52-week range percentile is a neutral 49, and Brent falling from $100.31 to $88.24 over the month removes the terms-of-trade offset that normally protects the Canadian dollar. The Bank of Canada meets on 2 September and 28 October and is expected to hold or ease, so the differential widens if the Fed hikes.

cleanest_bearish_expression.rationale: If the dollar view fails, AUD/USD is where it fails most expensively and therefore where the short-dollar expression is cleanest. Australia out-yields the US at both the policy rate (4.35% against 3.625%, worth -72.5bp of carry to the dollar) and the June-vintage 10-year (4.831% against 4.47%), so a dollar short is paid to hold. Spot at 0.71669 sits at the 87th percentile of its 52-week range with the pair above all four moving averages including the 200-week at 0.66471, Australian CPI at 3.96% keeps the RBA from cutting, and the BIS real effective rate of 115.92 versus the dollar's 107.84 makes the dollar 6.97% cheap in real terms against the Australian dollar - the second-largest negative real deviation the dollar carries.

relative_value_pairs.thesis: The purest carry-per-unit-of-risk trade in the set at 362.5bp against a zero SNB rate on 7.23% realised volatility, a ratio of 0.501. It is a relative-value rather than directional expression because it works on the differential alone: USD/CHF has appreciated 4.05% over six months despite the franc's safe-haven bid, and the SNB is anchored at the lower bound with no meeting until 24 September.

relative_value_pairs.pair: Long GBP/USD as the hedge to the tactical view
relative_value_pairs.thesis: Sterling is the only peer within 25bp of the dollar, at +12.5bp, and a 25bp hike on 16 September flips that to -12.5bp - the cleanest sign change in the set. That makes GBP/USD the most sensitive pair to the binary and therefore the most efficient place to hold the offsetting position if the Committee holds, with the Bank of England resolving its own decision the following day on 17 September.

relative_value_pairs.pair: Short USD/JPY as the strategic offset
relative_value_pairs.thesis: USD/JPY at 159.746 rests on a 180bp 10-year spread taken from a stale 2026-06-01 monthly vintage that materially understates Japan's live yield. The pair sits at the 77th percentile of its 52-week range on a foundation that is narrowing, which makes it the single largest carry-unwind exposure in the set and the natural strategic hedge against a tactical long-dollar book.

cross_horizon_consistency.summary: The horizons are not aligned: tactical Bullish at conviction 3 with a net score of +0.3440 against strategic Neutral at conviction 2 with +0.1032. The dollar ranks first of eleven over four weeks and fourth of eleven over six months.
cross_horizon_consistency.divergence_explanation: The divergence is mechanical, not a hedge, and it comes from the reweighting. Inflation and Growth falls from 0.18 to 0.10 and turns Neutral as the tariff-driven price impulse gives way to labour-market deterioration, while External Balance rises from 0.06 to 0.16 and turns Bearish, a swing of -0.0992 in the weighted contribution from a factor that contributes nothing tactically. Policy and Rates keeps its 0.24 weight but its confidence falls from 68 to 58 because the Committee's own June projections - a 2026 median of 3.8% and a 2027 median of 3.6% - make the September hike terminal rather than the start of a cycle.
cross_horizon_consistency.inflection_point: Late October to early November 2026. Specifically the 28 October FOMC, which is the first meeting after September without a Summary of Economic Projections attached and therefore the first at which the market must judge whether the hike was terminal on the Committee's silence rather than its dots.
cross_horizon_consistency.catalyst_for_transition: The 16 September dot plot itself is the transition catalyst, which is unusual: the same release that resolves the tactical trade also sets the strategic path. If the 2027 median holds at 3.6% the strategic Neutral is confirmed and the tactical position should be treated as having an expiry; if it is lifted above 3.6%, the September hike becomes a cycle and the strategic stance would be upgraded.
cross_horizon_consistency.trading_implication: Treat the tactical view as a trade with a defined expiry rather than as the opening leg of a strategic position. The practical instruction is to express the tactical view in one-month options expiring after 16 September, where the 5.357% implied volatility carries only a 0.72-point premium over realised, and to hold no residual outright strategic dollar exposure - expressing any strategic view through the relative-value pairs instead.
